test_title: RRB Group D Official Paper (Held On: 09 Dec, 2025 Shift 3)
subject: general
question: If a student adds water to a concentrated acid quickly, what is likely to happen?

options.text: The solution may splash and cause burns.

solution:
The correct answer is __**The solution may splash and cause burns**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• Mixing a concentrated acid with water is a highly **exothermic reaction**, meaning it releases a significant amount of **heat energy**. When water is added to a concentrated acid, the first drop of water reacts with a large excess of acid, generating intense heat locally. ***Hence, the statement "The solution may splash and cause burns" is correct.***
 
• If water is poured into **concentrated sulfuric acid**, the heat generated is so high that it can instantly convert the water into **steam**. This rapid expansion of steam can cause the acid to **splash out** of the container, potentially causing **severe chemical burns** on the skin or eyes of the person performing the experiment.
 
• Acids do not change their physical state to solid upon the addition of water; rather, they become **diluted**. The **solubility** of most common acids like **hydrochloric acid (HCl)** or **sulfuric acid (H2SO4)** increases or remains high in aqueous solutions. ***Hence, the statement "The acid will solidify" is incorrect.***
 
• Because the reaction is **exothermic**, the temperature of the mixture rises sharply. An **endothermic reaction** would be required for the solution to become cold, but the **enthalpy of hydration** for acid molecules is very high and negative. ***Hence, the statement "The solution will become cold" is incorrect.***
 
• Adding water to concentrated acid is never a neutral event; it is a hazardous chemical process that requires strict **safety protocols**. Ignoring the **chemical properties** of concentrated reagents can lead to laboratory accidents and **glassware breakage** due to **thermal shock**. ***Hence, the statement "Nothing will happen" is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Safety Protocol (The AA Rule):** The standard laboratory procedure is to always add **Acid to Aqua (Water)**, never the reverse. By adding **acid slowly** to a large volume of water while **stirring constantly**, the heat generated is distributed throughout the water, which has a **high specific heat capacity**, preventing the mixture from boiling or splashing.
 
• **Specific Heat Capacity:** Water has a high **specific heat capacity** of approximately **4.18 J/g°C**. This property allows it to absorb a significant amount of heat without a drastic increase in temperature, provided the acid is added in small, controlled increments.
 
• **Chemical Burns:** Concentrated acids are **corrosive substances** that can destroy body tissue. **Sulfuric acid** is particularly dangerous because it is also a **strong dehydrating agent**, meaning it removes water molecules from the proteins and lipids in human skin, causing deep **tissue damage**.
 
• **Hydration Energy:** The release of heat occurs because of the formation of **hydronium ions (H3O+)**. The process of **solvating** the acid molecules releases energy that was previously stored in the **chemical bonds**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Protective Gear:** When handling concentrated acids, it is mandatory to wear **Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)**, including **safety goggles**, **lab coats**, and **acid-resistant gloves** to mitigate the risk of accidental splashes.
 
• **Glassware Selection:** It is recommended to use **borosilicate glass** (like Pyrex) for dilutions, as it can withstand the **thermal expansion** caused by the **heat of solution** without cracking.
 
• **First Aid:** In the event of an **acid splash**, the affected area should be flushed immediately with **running water** for at least **15 to 20 minutes** to dilute and remove the chemical, followed by immediate medical consultation.
 
• **Concentration Levels:** A **concentrated acid** typically has a very low water content (e.g., **98% for Sulfuric Acid** or **37% for Hydrochloric Acid**), making the initial contact with water extremely reactive compared to **dilute acids**.
